extracted.intended_audience: artists, art historians, critics, and educated readers of art and architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for reading, composing, and judging architectural sculpture (especially Gothic vs Renaissance), including subject choice, naturalism, placement, durability, and symbolic/personifying practice. Focuses on how form, workmanship, and theological temperament are expressed in built sculpture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break the angle with enriched sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a building is nearly square, its sharp external angles must be softened or enriched (by groups of buttresses, turrets, niches, or sculpture) to avoid meagreness of effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "as the building was very nearly square on the ground plan, a peculiar prominence and importance were given to its angles, which rendered it necessary that they should be enriched and softened by sculpture...their effect depends on some modification of the sharpness of the angle, either by groups of buttresses, or by turrets and niches rich in sculpture." Use angle-decoration to relieve large wall surfaces and give architectural importance to corners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let architectural function inform decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Decorative choices (buttresses, pinnacles, towers at angles) should grow from the building's material, structural needs, and historical conditions (e.g., Gothic warfare), not be arbitrary ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Gothic principle "arising partly out of the necessity of strengthening the flanks of enormous buildings, where composed of imperfect materials, by buttresses or pinnacles; partly out of the conditions of Gothic warfare..."—i.e., form should answer material and functional conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the principal message at architectural focal points
rubrics_metrics.description: Major sculptural subjects belong on the 'corner stones' or architectural pivots (angles, principal capitals) because these spots communicate the builder's purpose, lesson, or sentiment most legibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "These, observe, are the very corner stones of the edifice, and in them we may expect to find the most important evidences of the feeling, as well as of the skill, of the builder...if he has anything to say to us of the purpose with which he built the palace, it is sure to be said here." Choose subjects at focal points to convey civic/religious meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject choice should express the spirit/temper of a school
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific narrative or allegory chosen (e.g., Fall of Man, Drunkenness of Noah, Judgment of Solomon) embodies the moral/spiritual temperament of the designers (Gothic humility vs Renaissance confident wisdom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "It is impossible to overstate...as if the palace had been built at various epochs...for the sole purpose of teaching us the difference in the temper of the two schools." Use subject matter intentionally to contrast ideological temperaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use naturalism in minor, structural vegetative elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalistic detail (leafage, tendrils, undercut veins) is especially appropriate and powerful in decorative natural elements; such fidelity to nature can be a work's most masterly feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The vine-leaf example: "he has literally carved every rib and vein upon them, in relief...the peculiar tessellated effect upon the eye." Plate choice favors refined naturalism in foliage as illustrative of Gothic naturalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance refinement with material durability
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme finesse in delicate elements may produce visual beauty but risks breakage and loss; designers must respect the material's limits and the sculpture's exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "the natural delicacy of the vine-leaf and tendril having tempted the sculptor to greater effort, he has passed the proper limits of his art, and cut the upper stems so delicately that half of them have been broken away..." Aim for an appropriate degree of finish given site and medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workmanship must make narrative legible
rubrics_metrics.description: Figurative sculpture should tell its story plainly; over-refinement or stiffness that obscures character or intent weakens communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "he has failed in telling his story plainly, regret and wonder being so equally marked on the features...that it is impossible to say which is intended for Ham." Legibility of expression is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider historical/stylistic accuracy as evidence and value
rubrics_metrics.description: Clothing, gestures, and physiognomy that match period types provide dating evidence and authenticity; proper historic detail enhances reading and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "the feet are protected simply by a bandage...a feature of dress which will be found in nearly every piece of figure sculpture in Venice, from the year 1300 to 1380"—use accurate period traits to situate works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse technical freedom with spiritual depth
rubrics_metrics.description: A composition may be freer or more accomplished in design but still be of "inferior spirit"—technical bravura does not substitute for truth to nature or moral/spiritual sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On Renaissance copy: "much more free in design...yet of immeasurably inferior spirit in the workmanship; the leaves...have none of its truth to nature." Evaluate both design freedom and inward spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use placement and small compositional gestures to indicate relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor figures and their proximity/gesture (e.g., Tobit following Raphael touching his hem) should reinforce the intended moral or devotional relationship (dependence, guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "this being...the general purpose of the introduction of the figures of the angels...intended to be more particularly conveyed by the manner in which the small figure of Tobit follows the steps of Raphael, just touching the hem of his garment." Small details communicate theological meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer symbolism for serious spiritual expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolism (imperfect sign pointing to a great truth) is the more appropriate device for serious, faithful religious representation, while personification risks reducing the sacred to fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Symbolism is the setting forth of a great truth by an imperfect and inferior sign...Men who use symbolism forcibly are almost always true believers in what they symbolize...Personification is the bestowing of a human or living form upon an abstract idea...apt to disturb the belief in the reality of the thing personified." Use symbols when aiming for spiritual depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personification cautiously and only when spiritually sincere
rubrics_metrics.description: Personification can be noble in early, earnest hands where faith underlies the image; otherwise it tends to be recreational and less noble than symbolism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "in the hands of its early and earnest masters...personification is, often thoroughly noble and lovely"—nobility depends on the sincerity and spiritual grounding of the artist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the appropriate set of virtues/personifications for context
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection and arrangement of virtues (cardinal, theological, local variations) should suit the subject/context (monastic, civic, funerary) rather than be an arbitrary classical reassembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giotto's differing systems at Assisi vs Arena Chapel illustrate adapting virtues to the life portrayed: "systems vary with almost every writer, and in almost every important work of art..." Tailor allegory to the intended audience and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial systematization that clouds meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Forcing classical moral systems onto Christian subjects or over-classifying virtues can produce confusion and inaccuracy; clarity of feeling is preferable to scholastic quibbling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "the mischief produced...by the mere habit of reading Aristotle...the study of it...is quite enough to occasion the utter want of accurate habits of thought...Aristotle mistakes Prudence...for the essence of the virtues themselves." Beware pedantic system-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose decorative elements into an 'unbroken line' when fitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Where vertical architectural features exist (arcades, shafts, niches), sculptural elements may be arranged in continuous vertical succession to form an integrated decorative line from ground to top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "thus forming an unbroken line of decoration from the ground to the top of the angle." Plan sequences (capital → figure → pillar → niche) to produce cohesive reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sculptures readable at intended viewing distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Works placed at about eight feet above eye-level should be 'read like the pages of a book' by habitual observers; scale and detail must suit expected viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "being at a height of little more than eight feet above the eye, might be read, like the pages of a book, by those...who habitually walked beneath the shadow of this great arcade"—ensure clarity for the audience's typical vantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let moral/affective tone determine representational mode
rubrics_metrics.description: The overarching affect (consciousness of human frailty vs confidence in wisdom) should shape subject matter, iconography, and stylistic choices rather than mere fashion or novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text contrasts Gothic "frank confession of its own weakness" with Renaissance "firm confidence in its own wisdom" and links those temperaments to sculptural subjects (Fall, Drunkenness vs Solomon). Choose modes that manifest the intended moral tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit natural forms as structural terminals
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural motifs (trees, vines) can be made structural—tree trunks forming the true outer angle, branches enwrapping sides—to integrate ornament with architecture and provide noble terminal groups of lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Its trunk...forms the true outer angle of the palace; boldly cut separate from the stone-work behind, and branching out above the figures so as to enwrap each side of the angle..." Use organic forms to define architectural junctions.
